data.title: Transaction
data.tagline: A group of related database operations that are committed or rolled back as a whole
data.learningOutcome: You can decide which database changes belong in one transaction and verify that a failure does not leave a partial update.
data.description: When an order is created, the system usually writes the order record and deducts inventory together. If stock is unavailable, the order should not remain. A transaction rolls back this group of operations in the same database, but it does not automatically undo external actions like payments or emails.

learning.assumes: You know that an order and inventory can be stored as separate database records.
learning.outcome: You can decide which database changes belong in one transaction and verify that a failure does not leave a partial update.

distinctions.label: Atomicity
distinctions.explanation: Atomicity is a core ACID property guaranteeing all-or-nothing execution; a Transaction is the full database boundary providing this guarantee.

distinctions.label: Database Write
distinctions.explanation: A Database Write persists records; a Transaction establishes the commit and rollback boundary for multi-step writes.

explanation.title: Problem and key mechanism
explanation.text: When order creation and inventory deduction are handled separately, a stock failure can leave an incomplete order behind. Putting both in the same transaction ensures that if either step fails, all order and inventory changes are rolled back.

explanation.title: How to observe the improvement
explanation.text: Commit the order and inventory changes together only after both succeed. Return the order ID on success, and return a specific reason on failure instead of presenting partial work as success.

explanation.title: Clinic booking also needs a transaction
explanation.text: Creating an appointment record and reserving the doctor's time slot belong in the same transaction. If the slot is unavailable, both roll back so no appointment is left without a slot.

data.boundary: A transaction usually protects operations within the same database. External payments, emails, and other services do not roll back automatically and need separate status tracking or compensation design.

lessonPractice.title: Inventory deduction fails, but the page already reports success. How should the flow be fixed?

options.label: Put order creation and inventory deduction in one transaction; roll back and return a failure if needed
options.feedback: Correct. Both database changes share the same commit boundary, so a failed deduction will not leave an incomplete order behind.

options.label: Save the order first, then write a cancellation record if inventory fails
options.feedback: These are still separate writes. Writing a cancellation record later can briefly expose an incorrect state and does not provide a shared commit boundary.

options.label: Show success after the order write and leave the inventory failure in logs
options.feedback: The page would show an incomplete order as successful to the user, and logging the error does not undo the database change.

data.agentPrompt: Inspect the checkout flow and put order creation and inventory deduction in the same database transaction. Simulate an inventory deduction failure and verify that neither an order record nor partial inventory changes remain. Commit and return the order ID only when both succeed. Do not assume external payments or emails will roll back automatically.
